Quantifying complexity within quantum field theory remains a formidable challenge, primarily due to the difficulty of moving past free models and their associated Gaussian states and operations. Our approach addresses this by examining conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, offering a comprehensive analysis of complexity for both states and operators within the universal sector of their energy-momentum tensor. Central to our framework are the Euler-Arnold equations and their integro-differential extensions, which ensure the optimization problem between arbitrary states or transformations is well-defined. This work expands upon the findings detailed in arXiv:2005.02402, elaborating on the derivation techniques employed. Key areas of focus include the application of differential regularization, solving the integro-differential equation governing Fubini-Study state complexity, and investigating the underlying geometric structure. Our results demonstrate that 1+1 dimensional conformal states achieve a maximum Fubini-Study complexity rate, a limit that is ultimately governed by an infrared cutoff. Furthermore, we establish that the optimal strategy to maximize this rate involves a state-slicing protocol. Notably, we confirm that in dimension 1+1, the Fubini-Study complexity rate is always concave, always non-decreasing, and bounded above. Additionally, we derive the equations describing Lab-Frames, which correspond to state complexity rate boosts, and define a world-line for the state along with an associated proper-time parameter. Our findings also yield a explicit formula for the Feman-Hellings-Oolinski (FHO) complexity, linking it directly to the 1+1 dimensional state complexity. The state complexity, proper-time, and Lab-Frame concepts are generalized to the universal sector of any 2-dimensional quantum state. Finally, we provide a rigorous proof for the triangle inequality of proper-time complexity and offer an explicit expression for the 1+1 dimensional operator complexity when formulated in terms of state complexity.

This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating high accuracy in reproducing LES-derived reaction rate fluctuations. Subsequently, the linearized governing equations, including the linearized EBU model for reaction rates, were solved for incoming acoustic perturbations. The resulting response modes align with previously observed experimentally and numerically modes, such as low-frequency "p" modes and high-frequency "q" modes. Furthermore, the linearized EBU model successfully predicted reaction rate oscillations for oblique modes, confirming its suitability. These findings validate the a priori linearization approach and the selected EBU model, indicating that this methodology can be utilized to investigate reaction rate oscillations in other turbulent combustion configurations. Additionally, this linearized model serves as a valuable tool for exploring reaction rate fluctuations in various setups through linear stability analysis. The underlying code, named TurbCombustionResponse, is accessible at: https://github.com/Jan-BernhardRueger/TurbCombustionResponse. These results support the conclusion that LES can be employed for further investigations into thermoacoustic instabilities in the specific configuration under consideration.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, when applied to the gravitational collapse of a spherical dust cloud, the nonlocal elements result in a deceleration of collapse; consequently, the maximum mass achievable before black hole formation is greater than the prediction made by local gravity. To investigate this phenomenon numerically, a model incorporating an exponential constitutive relation is employed. The findings indicate that for an Neumann-Pechac mass of $2.03\times$ the critical value (approximately $5.7$ solar masses), the nonlocal effects delay black hole creation by a factor of two relative to local predictions. Revisiting the constitutive relation for NLG in the context of quantum gravity, it is concluded that such a relation is incompatible with certain modern approaches, including asymptotic safety, string theory, and the Oxford formulation. In contrast, the fundamental formulation of NLG developed here is compatible with an effective field theory of gravity that includes tetrads and is nonlocal in time. This compatibility allows for a formal derivation of the constitutive relation, assuming the kernel takes a specific causal form. Based on observational constraints regarding the maximum mass of collapsing stars and the structure of the kernel, the constitutive relation for NLG exhibits stronger nonlocal characteristics than previously anticipated. Finally, the article examines how the kernel's structure influences the deceleration of stellar collapse and identifies the theoretical upper limit for the Neumann-Pechac mass.

Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel method that integrates prior strategies with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) architectures. Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior performance by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research. Finally, we devised countermeasures to mitigate this end-to-end threat and validated their efficacy. Given that HyperDegrade enables side-channel attacks to succeed where they previously failed without countermeasures, we conclude by providing detailed leakage models and estimating the minimum degradation required to bypass DDSE model-based countermeasures.

An unknotting operation represents a local modification applied to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Our findings indicate that the unknotting distance measured by the diagonal move for a knot is directly related to its Alexander polynomial and Jones polynomial. To support these conclusions, we provide specific examples and establish relevant theorems. The concept of the diagonal move and its associated distance can also be extended to links, allowing for the introduction of a 4-move distance for links under the classical and welding equivalences. Our results reveal that, for two-class links, the unknotting distance under the diagonal move and the 4-move equivalence are equivalent under both classical and welding equivalences. As an application, we generalize the unknotting distance for classical links to welded links under the diagonal move. Throughout this work, we consistently utilize Gaston General's knot software [1] for all calculations and visualizations concerning knots and links. The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. This configuration creates a triply-coupled cavity system capable of surpassing the loss-induced high-frequency limit inherent to signal-recycled Michelson interferometers. Using parameters comparable to advanced LIGO+, a sloshing-Sagnac design could achieve sevenfold improved sensitivity at 2.5 kHz, or a fourfold increase in signal-to-noise ratio for typical post-merger binary neutron star waveforms. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories.

This study investigates potential global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified General Circulation Model (GCM) derived from the University of Hamburg's Portable University Model for the Atmosphere. The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction, Newtonian cooling, and dry convective adjustment. Through a series of controlled experiments, researchers varied the planetary rotation rate and the imposed equator-to-pole temperature gradient. These variables were converted into dimensionless parameters to define a parameter space where distinct circulation regimes are identified and categorized. Significant trends emerge when altering the planetary rotation rate alongside frictional and thermal relaxation timescales. The progression of changes with respect to planetary rotation rate mirrors observations made when modifying the Coriolis force in a beta-plane model on the beta-plane parameter space. These findings support the conclusion that friction and radiative/convective relaxation timescales scale linearly with planetary rotation rate to maintain circulation velocities near those found on Earth. Additionally, the results indicate that mean zonal winds scale with the Rossby deformation radius rather than the Rossby number, particularly at Rossby numbers greater than 0.1. On an Earth-like planet, these dynamics generate a dominant midlatitude planetary wave number of 3, aligning with observed baroclinic eddy activity. These discoveries offer guidance for future searches for extraterrestrial atmospheric bands on planets with different rotational characteristics and provide theoretical backing for the existence of baroclinic eddies, planetary waves, and midlatitude eddies on gas giant planets like Jupiter and Saturn. Finally, these results have significant implications for selecting appropriate initial conditions and parameterizations in climate change studies on Earth and in simulations of planetary atmospheres with varying characteristics. Furthermore, these findings counter the common assumption that turbulent mixing becomes independent of rotation rate at very slow rotations (low Rossby numbers) on gas giants, an assumption underlying estimates of methane mixing timescales on Jupiter.

This study presents a real integral formulation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function using a regularized hypersingular integral. Hydrodynamic theories provide effective strategies for simulating the complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems that are otherwise computationally challenging. In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. This approach surpasses current hydrodynamic models, including superfluid and generalized hydrodynamics, by enabling the simulation of complete quantum dynamics; it can calculate non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even at short wavelengths. Based on this framework, we formulate a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme that extends the simulation duration for non-equilibrium scenarios beyond the limits of the full positive-P method, though this involves approximating quantum fluctuations. We demonstrate that this linearized scheme aligns directly with established Bogoliubov methods. Additionally, we validate the utility and benefits of this formalism by investigating correlations in a quantum shock wave scenario and contrasting its predictions with other standard quantum many-body approaches. These results highlight the capacity to assess quantum fluctuations in diverse scenarios, assess the validity ranges of various theories, and guide the creation of even more effective models for specific situations. Code access is available at https://github.com/evansar/POSQHD.

While Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at addressing large-scale problems across numerous domains, their deployment in real-time systems is often hindered by the sheer volume of parameters involved. To overcome this challenge, Teacher-Student architectures were initially introduced in the context of knowledge distillation, enabling lightweight student networks to match the performance of complex teacher models. Recently, these architectures have been widely adopted for diverse knowledge learning tasks, including knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Leveraging such frameworks, recent research has successfully achieved multiple learning objectives through efficient and compact student networks. Unlike previous surveys focused solely on knowledge distillation, this review comprehensively examines Teacher-Student architectures across a spectrum of knowledge learning goals. Furthermore, we systematically outline the processes of knowledge construction and optimization, analyze various architectural designs and learning strategies used to acquire representative and robust knowledge, and summarize recent applications in classification, recognition, and generation. Finally, we explore future research directions concerning architecture design, knowledge quality, and theoretical advancements in regression-based learning. By providing a thorough overview, this survey offers valuable insights and practical guidelines for both industry professionals and the academic community regarding Teacher-Student architectures in multi-objective knowledge learning. The complete text of this survey is available at arXiv:2201.02900.

We introduce a new, compact representation for graphical models, a foundational framework for numerous reasoning tasks. We refer to this enhanced approach as FABE. Incorporating our compact representation into FABE significantly speeds up BE execution; based on experiments with a classic robotic scenario and the Funsix game, we anticipate that FABE will solve most probable explanation (MPE) problems under constraints roughly 100,000 times faster than current methods. Beyond optimizing algorithms, this representation also facilitates quicker construction of graphs for information management, enabling optimizations distinct from FABE. Consequently, our concise graphical representation offers benefits across various inference and optimization applications. Aligning with recent trends in artificial intelligence, this "neuro-symbolic" representation could also support optimization problems in neural networks, such as training word embeddings. Significance testing, particularly the paired-permutation test, has been essential for ensuring that performance differences between NLP systems are statistically significant rather than due to chance. This paper introduces an efficient exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test applicable to a specific family of structured test statistics. The proposed algorithm operates in $\mathcal{O}(GN (\log GN )(\log N ))$ time, where $N$ represents the dataset size and $G$ denotes the range of the test statistic. Experimental results indicate that our exact algorithm is 10 times faster than a Monte Carlo approximation using 20,000 samples on a standard dataset. Furthermore, the algorithm scales effectively on larger datasets; for instance, processing a dataset of 10,000 sentences takes only 2 minutes. This exact algorithm enables researchers to explore non-parametric significant testing methods beyond the paired-permutation test within its specific context. Regarding the context of NLG evaluation, the author hopes this work encourages the investigation of this algorithm with state-of-theart evaluators to determine if significant differences exist between various evaluators when assessing agree ment on datasets like CEVAL (Brasseau et al., 2019) or XSL (Rushton et al., 2018). Additionally, the exact algorithm could help system authors understand the sample requirements needed for performance differences to achieve statistical significance when making claims about the superiority of their system's evaluator on a dataset via an NLG metric significance test. Finally, the author anticipates that data scientists in business or medical sectors will also find applications for this algorithm in A\/B testing for recommendation tasks, such as determining if one algorithm outperforms another in email suggestions or medical treatment plans. To support this, an open-source implementation in C++ and R is available at https://github.com/yvshar/exact_pairwise_permutation_test.

Soccer is a game characterized by sparse rewards, where even intelligent or negligent decisions in pivotal moments can alter the match outcome. Consequently, players, coaches, and scouts seek to identify the optimal actions during critical phases, such as high-risk scenarios involving potential loss of possession or scoring opportunities. This study introduces a novel state representation for soccer combined with batch reinforcement learning to train a policy network capable of determining the best action in any given situation. The approach incorporates an attention mechanism to assist the policy in focusing on the ball's location and the nearest opponents or teammates. Additionally, an action selection mechanism is added to ensure the policy generates desirable behaviors, including exploring new states. Using an open-source dataset of real-time tracking data from the UEFA Champions League, the model was trained on matches involving the Bavarian club Bayern Munich over the 2017/18 and 2018/19 seasons. Evaluation against a greedy network in the same dataset demonstrated that the trained policy consistently outperformed the greedy approach, yielding an average benefit of +0.133 benefits per state. Furthermore, the policy successfully derived near-optimal strategies for specific teams within the dataset, successfully integrating all recommended actions into their in-game playstyles. The developed state representation, policy network, and action selection mechanism are entirely data-independent, allowing application to other sparsely rewarded games like basketball or American football. Source code and the trained model will be made available at https://github.com/Ahmed-Elsherif99/Optimized_Soccer_Policy.

We derive an explicit description of both the spectral and orbital stability for solitary wave solutions to the one-dimensional $\mathbf{U}(1)$-invariant Klein--Gordon equation, which is coupled to an anharmonic oscillator. Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of the spectrum resulting from the linearization around these solitary waves. Our findings reveal that a mode with a positive eigenvalue, corresponding to linear instability, emerges once the wave amplitude surpasses a specific threshold. This result contradicts previous claims which suggested the linearized operator around the $\mathbf{U}(1)$-invariant solitary waves in the ANZ model \cite{ANZ79} was positive definite. Finally, we demonstrate that despite being linearly unstable, these solitary waves remain orbitally stable.

At colliders, neutral long-lived particles are identified either via displaced decay products or as missing energy, with the optimal search strategy depending on both the detector characteristics and the particle's decay length. We introduce a novel approach to detect two-body decays characterized by $B^+ \to K^+ a$ followed by $a\to E\!\!\!/$, where $E\!\!\!/$ represents missing energy. Utilizing an integrated luminosity of $50\,$ab$^{-1}$, Belle II is capable of probing light invisible resonances with branching ratios $\mathcal{B}(B^+\to K^+ a) \gtrsim 10^{-7}$ and decay lengths $c\tau_a \gtrsim 1\,$m. For axion-like particles, we anticipate that the sensitivity of the $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ channel to small couplings could improve by up to two orders of magnitude relative to prior searches at fixed-target and collider facilities. Specifically, for sub-GeV particles, the combination of $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ at Belle II and beam-dump experiments offers the greatest sensitivity, whereas for heavier particles, the smallest couplings can be probed through displaced vertex searches at Belle II, long-lived particle studies at the LHC, and future fixed-target experiments. As a direct consequence of this analysis, we rule out a recent prediction positing that neutrino oscillations can generate observable displaced vertices at beam-dump experiments if the oscillation probability is converted into missing energy via the decay $nu_3\to mu^+ W^- \to mu^+ a^+ a^-$.

In the early 1930s, K. Menger explored the concept of an abstract angle function, defining it broadly for metric and semi-metric spaces. He also formulated two challenges regarding the conformal embeddability of spaces equipped with an angle function into Euclidean spaces. Although these problems garnered attention later, solutions were limited to specific instances of metric spaces. This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. First, we establish an equivalence between the existence of a valid Euclidean angle function for a given space $(X,\alpha)$ and its conformal embeddability into $\R^n$ (where the function values are constrained to $[0,\pi]$). Second, leveraging a result by A. D. Aleksandrov on embedding spaces with a betweenness relation, we answer the question of when such a space (where the angle function takes values in $[0,\pi]$) can be embedded into Euclidean space. Finally, we address an inquiry from the problems by Menger concerning the simultaneous embeddability of two distinct angle functions into Euclidean space. Our solution relies on the first problem's result and utilizes a contribution by J. R. Simon and the author. Throughout this work, we also incorporate several other prior results. Notably, our approach does not require the angle function to be strictly positive, thus responding affirmatively to a question raised by J. van Leeuwen and C. van den Berg. The formal definition begins with the following: a betweenness relation on a set $X$ is a symmetric ternary operation $B(X)$ satisfying $B(x,x,y)=B(x,y,x)$, along with additional conditions.

Subsequently, we define specialized certification protocols for various specific semantic transformations and their combinations. These compatibility results highlight how different explicit theories of local class field theory can be interconnected. Furthermore, we provide an explicit version of these laws that incorporates the higher cocycles central to Abrashkin's work. Our derivation of Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' result from theirs (in the general context) also utilizes these higher cocycles. Fiber-reinforced composites featuring nanofiller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are highly effective at identifying the existence of damage, they struggle to deliver accurate details regarding the damage's shape, dimensions, or underlying mechanism. This limitation is especially problematic for laminated composites, which are prone to complex failure modes such as delaminations that are challenging to identify. To address this, we introduce a novel method for precisely determining the shape and size of damage in self-sensing composites. Our approach combines a genetic algorithm with realistic physics-based damage models to reconstruct accurate damage geometry from conductivity variations captured via EIT. We experimentally validated this technique using carbon nanofiber (CNF)-reinforced glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates, focusing on two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.25 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. These findings indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based spatial imaging and physics-based inversion strategies can enable precise damage shape reconstruction in self-sensing composite structures.

We demonstrate how to construct a metric tensor that converts between vectors and second-rank tensors, enabling the derivation of scalar products and the formulation of a Euclidean magnitude for second-rank tensors. Finally, we extend this methodology to three-dimensional space, defining an orientation operator (an antisymmetric second-rank tensor) and deriving the associated vector identities. This work underscores the significance of Euclidean vector concepts when describing second-rank tensors in Euclidean spaces. Specifically, in $\mathbb{R}^2$, the set of symmetric second-rank tensors is isomorphic to the set of 2D vectors, while in $\mathbb{R}^3$, the set of antisymmetric second-rank tensors is isomorphic to the set of 3D vectors. This research serves as a foundational study emphasizing the importance of these concepts in specific domains, such as the theory of elasticity.

We demonstrate that if a right-angled Artin group $A(\Gamma)$ admits a non-trivial, minimal action on a tree $T$ that is not a line, then $\Gamma$ must contain a separating subgraph $\Lambda$ for which $A(\Lambda)$ stabilizes an edge in $T$. Consequently, all minimal actions on trees arise from the splitting of $A(\Gamma)$ along an edge or over an amalgamated product. This confirms a hypothesis by Caprace and Valette. Additionally, we explicitly characterize when right-angled Artin groups decompose as free products or as non-trivial amalgamated products. As applications, we provide a complete description of their fixed point sets on $\mathcal{PT}$ and $\mathcal{CT}$, and determine when these groups are rigid. Furthermore, considering a sequence of such groups where each lacks a cyclic factor, we establish necessary conditions for convergence to the Bass-Serre boundary. These conditions are sufficient in the case of free groups, yielding a Mod-$p$ application for right-angled Artin groups. Our results also clarify the assumptions required for the "proof" of the Outer Conjecture for these groups by Delgado, Dru{\c{c}}u, and Samet. The main findings extend to $\righttita$-by-RAAGs, provided that the stabilizers of edges in the underlying graph of groups are themselves RAAGs (in our specific context, these are free products of sub-RAAGs). In particular, we apply these results to analyze the actions of right-angled Cremer groups on their associated right-angled building. The proof of the main theorem generalizes a result by Deligne, Brouwer, and Nicas for commutative groups and one by House for amenable groups. We also thank the unknown referees for suggestions that improved the main results and their extensions. If $\Gamma$ is a finite, simple graph, then $A(\Gamma)$ denotes the corresponding right-angled Artin group, where vertices represent generators and edges impose relations.

Advancements in technology have enabled big data processing, yet this has created substantial computational challenges when solving large-scale linear systems or performing matrix inversions. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method is stable only within a specific inception depth range, with the convergence rate optimally minimized at the inception depth's maximum value. Furthermore, the NN algorithm requires no initial preconditioning matrix inversion, as it is constructed directly from the target matrix. Comparative experiments against NI, CI, NS, and NN demonstrate convergence rates of 2, 3, 4, and 7 per iteration, respectively. Notably, the NN method achieves inversion accuracy with far fewer iterations than NI, CI, or NS. These results indicate that the NN technique provides an effective, high-performance solution for large sparse and semi-sparse positive semi-definite matrices, particularly when the product of the matrix's maximum eigenvalue and the NN's inception depth remains less than one. To this end, we propose a practical solution by dynamically determining the optimal inception depth based on the matrix's maximum eigenvalue. Additional findings show that NN iterations perform effectively even when the "inception depth × maximum eigenvalue" product exceeds one. Ultimately, the Nested Neumann method provides a powerful, high-order iterative tool for large matrix inversions, delivering rapid results with acceptable accuracy. This generalization of higher-order iterations of the target matrix within the NS framework ensures the NN approach remains a robust solution for inversions requiring high precision, such as linear regression. Ultimately, the NN method offers a compelling alternative to other iterative techniques for large-scale matrix inversions demanding high computational performance and accuracy. Regarding implementation, the code for this generalization of iterative matrix inversion via the Nested Neumann series is available at: https://github.com/harsh-dk/NestedNeumann.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor exceeding 10. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system.

This study examines harmonic functions defined on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons that possess constant scalar curvature. We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. As a consequence, we prove that the dimension of the space of harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth is finite. These findings are significant for the stability analysis of gradient shrinking solitons under the Ricci flow. The proof of the main liouville result utilizes Yau's classical approach, incorporating Bochner's formula, Robin's inequality, and a refined application of Li's argument. Furthermore, we conclude with an open problem regarding the potential for a novel Liouville theorem derived via comparison arguments. The paper also details a new result on Robin's inequality applicable to manifolds with non-negative sectional curvature and mean convex boundaries.

The rise of outsourced training and machine learning as a service has introduced new attack vectors, specifically backdoor attacks. These attacks conceal a secret function within a neural network that activates only when a specific trigger is present in the input. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a significant portion of poisoned training data. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks can occur with "bypass" triggers, which must remain invisible to the model during training yet become visible and functional at activation time. Surprisingly, this phenomenon can be achieved with a minuscule trigger of just three pixels per image. We attribute this capability to Global Average Pooling (GAP), a standard layer in nearly all practical neural network architectures that remains underutilized in security research. Our findings warn that until models are defended against such exploits at the architectural level, dynamic backdoor attacks with invisible bypass triggers will likely persist. To address this, we propose a countermeasure that prevents these attacks by transforming inputs into a domain where the anticipated exploit no longer occurs. Our experiments confirm this approach effectively stops dynamic backdoor attacks with invisible bypass triggers in both image and video datasets. Given the ubiquity of the GAP layer, these results hold significant importance for the security of deployed neural networks. The source code for our implementation and datasets is accessible at https://github.com/Prathamesh1709/DynamicBackdoor.

This work addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a model from data distributed across graph nodes, with Federated Learning (FL) serving as the primary application. A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and slow convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk (RW) learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize direct connections between nodes, which are typically more efficient than communicating with the PS. In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; ideally, nodes with more informative data should be visited more frequently. We formulate this as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to develop a near-optimal node sampling strategy that minimizes gradient estimate variance and asymptotically approaches optimal sampling. Building on this, we propose an adaptive random walk learning algorithm and provide theoretical convergence guarantees. Our numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results and demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses existing random walk methods. As a concluding real-world test, we apply our approach to a linguistic dataset, showing it effectively mitigates bottlenecks caused by text data heterogeneity. An open-source implementation of the algorithm and dataset is available at https://github.com/Prasanthi03/Walk_for_Learning. Key contributions include an image segmentation dataset from a real city and its linguistic counterpart, along with the algorithmic framework used to analyze it. Additional contributions are a prioritized random walk algorithm with proven convergence guarantees for real-world data with unknown distributions, and an adaptive random walk algorithm that achieves state-of-the-art performance on such data. Finally, we introduce a novel random walk approach with theoretical convergence guarantees capable of handling data distributions with heavy-tailed gradients.

Pixel-level annotation scarcity remains a significant challenge in medical image segmentation. To address this, we present a novel regularization approach utilizing interpolation-based mixing for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. This method employs a consistency regularization strategy that ensures the segmentation of interpolated pairs of unlabeled images aligns with the interpolation of their corresponding segmentation maps. As a form of data-adaptive regularization, it helps reduce overfitting to labeled data, particularly when confidence levels are high. Compared to adversarial and generative models, this approach offers the advantage of requiring no extra computational resources. Evaluations on two public MRI datasets, ACDC and MMWHS, show that our method outperforms existing semi-supervised models. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/harsh-1997/ICT-MedSeg. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis and modeling. Through a refined memory access scheme, the hardware supports complex matrix transformations in real-time without access conflicts. Evaluation results demonstrate that both the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the dedicated hardware accelerator deliver superior performance. Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on their compatibility with observed data to facilitate selection among competing models. Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, it is demonstrated that point estimates of Bayes factors derived from Monte Carlo samples do not converge to the correct value when likelihoods rely on maximum likelihood estimation, particularly with small sample sizes. The analysis also covers the influence of prior choices on Bayes factors and their associated utility scores. To address these challenges during practical application, we propose an automated workflow designed to support the reliable use of Bayes factors for hypothesis testing. This workflow comprises three stages: initial exploration via posterior probabilities and other metrics to assess the feasibility of Bayes factors; determination of an appropriate MCMC budget for accurate calculation; and final computation of the Bayes factor itself. To validate this approach, we applied the workflow to a real-world dataset from the cognitive science domain and confirmed its effectiveness through simulation. The proposed methodology serves as a valuable tool for researchers utilizing Bayes factors, ensuring more dependable statistical analysis. These proofs share significant similarities, yet existing presentations are scattered, overly complex, or lack necessary details for true comparability. Additionally, current demonstrations of Godel's and Rosser's theorems rely on specific properties of the standard diagonalization function. Consequently, neither Godel's first incompleteness theorem nor Rosser's theorem is truly "incompleteness" in the strict sense, as the diagonalization function itself is an unspecifiable arithmetic property required for the proof—a nuance lost in common terminology. This paper provides fully detailed, side-by-side proofs of Godel's numeral lemma, the first incompleteness theorem, Tarski's theorem, the Godel-Carnap diagonal lemma, and Rosser's theorem (which depends on the first theorem and the diagonal lemma). These accounts employ identical lemmas and theorems, utilize consistent notation, and follow a nearly paragraph-for-paragraph parallel structure. Although Godel's first incompleteness theorem and Rosser's theorem appear to depend on a particular diagonalization function, the proof actually relies only on three properties: it must be surjective, satisfy one side of the lemma's signature equation, and allow construction of a function with the lemma's specific signature equation (which need not be the original). This final characteristic is what defines the "diagonal" nature. With this understanding, we offer a proof of Godel's first incompleteness theorem that does not depend on any diagonalization, hence the title: Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem Without Requiring Diagonalization. All proofs in this work are elementary and demand no prior knowledge of Godelian methods. We anticipate this paper will serve as an ideal resource for teaching these theorems and proofs. This study addresses the identification of a missing boundary condition for a two-dimensional linear acoustic wave equation coupled with a Kirchhoff plate on a circular domain. For both continuous and discrete systems, we first establish unique solvability and finite-sample resolvability of the inverse problem via a Neumann series approach. Subsequently, an operator-based regularized iteration algorithm is developed to solve the inverse problem for the continuous model. Resolvability for the discrete model is ensured through the regularized iteration method, and the algorithm's effectiveness is validated with numerical examples. Finally, a regularized quasi-Reverse Time Finite Difference (RTFD) approach is applied to handle noise in boundary measurements, with results confirmed by experiments using a water tank. These findings suggest that the regularized RTFD algorithm can effectively reconstruct the unknown boundary condition from noisy data, even when the condition itself depends on time derivatives of the noise. The resulting reconstruction is smooth and free of artifacts, suggesting significant potential for this method in real-world applications.

This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical plan to investigate this model at particle accelerators and underground detectors. Specifically, the research conducts a comprehensive search for dark matter within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework, detailing a coherent spectrum of new particles and their masses. A primary focus is placed on analyzing the phenomenology of weak-scale mass parameters and neutrino mixing angles, particularly regarding direct detection limits, LHC constraints, dark matter relic density, and consistency within the Standard Model sector (including electroweak vacuum stability and neutrless beta decay limits). The study evaluates the probability of finding a dark matter solution across all parameter space, particularly concerning dark matter direct detection and LHC constraints versus the thermally derived relic density. Finally, it investigates the probabilities of achieving neutrino mixing and mass spectrum predictions that align with observed data. In search of globally stable dark matter relic solutions, the analysis highlights a significant inverse correlation between the top quark pole mass ($M_{t,pole}$) and the dark matter density ($\Omega_{DM}h^{2}$), similar to findings in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model.
